::: {.flashcard-page}

The first thing that surprised me about Rust variables was that a plain `let`
does not give me something I can freely reassign. Rust makes the safer choice
the short choice.

::: {.flashcard-stage}
::: {.flashcard-card}
<div class="flashcard-meta">
  <span class="flashcard-number">Flashcard 03</span>
  <span class="flashcard-topic">Rust</span>
</div>

<div class="flashcard-eyebrow">The question</div>

::: {#flashcard-question .flashcard-question role="heading" aria-level="2"}
Why can’t I assign a new value to this variable?
:::

<p class="flashcard-hint">Look at the binding. A plain <code>let</code> carries an important default.</p>

<details class="flashcard-reveal">
  <summary>Reveal the answer</summary>
<div class="flashcard-answer"><p>Rust bindings are immutable by default. Add <code>mut</code> when the value must change, or use a new <code>let</code> when shadowing is what you mean.</p></div>
</details>
:::
:::

## Immutable by default

The keyword `let` creates a binding:

```rust
fn main() {
    let name = "unrahul";
    println!("name is {}", name);
}
```

```text
name is unrahul
```

If I try to assign another value to `name`, the compiler stops me:

```rust
fn main() {
    let name = "unrahul";
    println!("name is {}", name);
    name = "rahul";
    println!("new name is {}", name);
}
```

```text
error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `name`
  |
2 |     let name = "unrahul";
  |         ---- first assignment to `name`
3 |     name = "rahul";
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable
```

::: {.flashcard-block .flashcard-block--compiler}
<p class="flashcard-block-label">A useful compiler follow-up</p>

Running `rustc --explain E0384` gives a longer explanation of this exact error.
The compiler error codes are worth following.
:::

## Make the binding mutable

When reassignment is actually part of the program, I can say so explicitly:

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut name = "unrahul";
    println!("name is {}", name);
    name = "rahul";
    println!("new name is {}", name);
}
```

```text
name is unrahul
new name is rahul
```

The only change is `let mut name`. Anyone reading the code can now see that the
binding may change.

## Shadow the old binding

Shadowing creates a new binding with the same name:

```rust
fn main() {
    let name = "unrahul";
    println!("name is {}", name);

    let name = "rahul";
    println!("new name is {}", name);
}
```

```text
name is unrahul
new name is rahul
```

That second `let` is not mutating the first binding. It creates a new one and
shadows the old `name`. The new binding may even have a different type, which
is one reason shadowing is not the same thing as `mut`.

::: {.flashcard-block .flashcard-block--remember}
<p class="flashcard-block-label">What I keep in my head</p>

Use `mut` when one binding changes value. Use another `let` when I want a new
binding that happens to reuse the same name.
:::
